messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolk,

New versions of the Distance and mrds R packages are now on CRAN. Binary
packages for Windows/Mac may take a while to appear. Changes are listed
below.

cheers,
--dave

---

Distance 1.0.2 NEWS:

* ds.gof is now deprecated for goodness-of-fit testing. gof_ds is now
preferred.
* add_df_covar_line (actually located in mrds) can now plot probability
density functions for point transects
* bootdht can now use the progress package if installed to give an
estimated time remaining for bootstraps (option
progress_bar="progress"). Alternatively no progress bar can be shown
with progress_bar="none".

mrds 2.2.4 NEWS:

* add_df_covar_line now plots probability density functions for the
point transect case
* warning is no longer raised when truncation is not set but bins are
specified for binned data (it's assumed that the furthest cutpoint is
the truncation)
* AIC/logLik functions now work for all methods

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Model design for post stratification in r
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Model design for post stratification in r
messages.body_plain:
Sam

I've spend some more time working with your data set.  The options "replicate" and "effort_sum" don't produce reasonable degrees of freedom for your survey-specific estimates, so for the moment, those options are not to be considered.

If your interest lies in examining density or abundance of your birds over time (and wish to ignore the average estimates across all surveys), then I suggest you use "geographical" as your stratification option (ignoring the Total across all surveys).  Furthermore, you note the small number of replicate points and the small number of detections made during some of the time periods, making inference for some of those surveys dubious.

I've analysed the data pooling some of the surveys to enhance the robustness of the estimates.  Not knowing your study objectives, it is dangerous for me to make decisions about combining surveys.  I combined the Feb19 and Apr19 surveys into a single "spring19" survey;  Jul19 and Sep19 combined into "summer19"; Nov19 and Jan20 into "winter19" and Jun20 through Oct20 into "summer20".  In addition to including those surveys as covariates in the detection function, I also included group size (as your detections were of bird groups).

The model fits well and might provide robust estimates through time, if not at the temporal granularity you desire.

Code below.  Note the probability density function plots (showing the survey effect) will only work if you download the most recent version of Distance from CRAN.

library(Distance)
sam <- read.csv("C:/Users/erexs/Downloads/sampoints.csv")
sam$object <- NULL
unit_conversion_point <- convert_units("meter", NULL, "hectare")
season <- sam
season$month <- month(as.Date.character(sam$Survey_Date, format = "%d/%m/%Y"))
sp19 <- ifelse(season$month==2 | season$month==4, TRUE, FALSE)
sum19 <- ifelse(season$month==7 | season$month==9, TRUE, FALSE)
win19 <- ifelse(season$month==11 | season$month==1, TRUE, FALSE)
sum20 <- ifelse(season$month==6 | season$month==8 | season$month==10, TRUE, FALSE)
season$Region.Label[sp19] <- "sp19"
season$Region.Label[sum19] <- "sum19"
season$Region.Label[win19] <- "win19"
season$Region.Label[sum20] <- "sum20"
season.only <- ds(season, transect = "point", key="hn",adjustment = NULL,
           formula=~Region.Label, truncation=160,
           convert.units = unit_conversion_point)
season.size <- ds(season, transect = "point", key="hn",adjustment = NULL,
               formula=~Region.Label+size, truncation=160,
               convert.units = unit_conversion_point)
gof_ds(season.only, plot = FALSE)
gof_ds(season.size, plot = FALSE)
AIC(season.only, season.size)
plot(season.size, pdf=TRUE, showpoints=FALSE, main="Season and size as covariates")
add_df_covar_line(season.size, data=data.frame(Region.Label="sp19", size=1),
                  lwd=2, col="blue", pdf=TRUE)
add_df_covar_line(season.size, data=data.frame(Region.Label="sum19", size=1),
                  lwd=2, col="red", pdf=TRUE)
add_df_covar_line(season.size, data=data.frame(Region.Label="win19", size=1),
                  lwd=2, col="green", pdf=TRUE)
add_df_covar_line(season.size, data=data.frame(Region.Label="sum20", size=1),
                  lwd=2, col="darkgreen", pdf=TRUE)
legend("topright", title="Season", legend=c("win19","sp19","sum19","sum20"),
       col=c("green","blue","red","darkgreen"),
       lwd=2)
season.size.dht2 <- dht2(season.size, flatfile=season, strat_formula = ~Region.Label,
                    stratification = "geographical",sample_fraction = 0.5, total_area = 222.5,

                    ci_width = 0.95, convert_units = unit_conversion_point)

print(season.size.dht2, report="density")

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] CTDS - impact of deviation from predefined snapshot moment
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] CTDS - impact of deviation from predefined snapshot moment
messages.body_plain:
Olly, I think bias would vary substantially from one application to another.  It will be a strong function of how animals move for example.  But it seems to me that you might be asking the wrong question.  I can’t see the variation in gaps between images within a burst being an issue, but what is an issue is separation between one burst and the next.  If your snapshot moments were entirely independent of what animals are doing, the gap between snapshot moments could be whatever you choose.  If you choose a long gap, there would be fewer images to store and analyse, but also fewer detections, so it would be a compromise which affects precision and cost but not bias.  However, if you only take images when an animal is present, then the snapshot separation needs to be short, so that animals cannot pass in front of the camera without being recorded.  For a given animal pass, you can define the first snapshot moment to be the moment the camera first triggers.  Then you would want it to trigger again 2s later – or whatever time separation you have selected.  I don’t see why you would select burst mode, as you would then want the next burst starting immediately.  So why not have the camera in single-image mode, and set so that it triggers every 2s (say) until the animal has passed out of the detection area?  If your animals are slow-moving and detectable at large distances, you could have much longer than 2s between snapshot moments.

Sent: 04 December 2020 09:53
To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [distance-sampling] CTDS - impact of deviation from predefined snapshot moment

Hi list,

In Howe et al. 2017, the authors discuss selection of pre-defined snapshot moments, typically in 2 second increments past the minute (e.g. 08:03:00, 08:03:02, 08:03:04, ... 08:03:58 etc). This is done to avoid bias in animal detection distances, which could occur due to the conical shape of the field of view of a camera trap. To quote:

"Observed distances upon first detection are expected to be positively biased because animals entering the detection zone through the arc of the sector would contribute a disproportionate number of observations at far distances. Bias would be slight if the time between snapshot moments (t) was small enough to ensure that the animals did not move far relative to the range of the sensor between snapshots, as then the observations would be representative of animals’ continuous paths past the CTs. However, we prefer to avoid the potential for bias by assuming that the snapshot moments are selected independently of animal locations, and predetermining them as specific times of day to ensure that the assumption is met."

This effect is illustrated in Eric's PhD thesis in more detail (see Figure 3.1): Howe, E. J. (2019). Estimating abundance of African great apes. University of St Andrews. Available from http://hdl.handle.net/10023/18859.

In Cappelle et al. 2019, the authors state they used a t  of 2 seconds, but from the start of each captured video, rather than predetermined based on time of day:

"We recorded observation distances between cameras and the midpoints of each filmed chimpanzee at 2‐s intervals (i.e., at 0, 2, 4, …, 58 s after the start of the video),  independent of whether single individuals or groups were seen."

Despite this, this CTDS survey produced accurate results compared to other survey methods and to the known size of chimpanzee groups. Talking with Noémie, she thought that with a t of 2s, the difference between using snapshots defined from time vs from video start would be small.

This leads to my main question, which is: is there any estimate available on the size of this potential bias?

I'll explain the context of my question in relation to our planned survey, in case this has a bearing on the answer...

We plan to use photo captures, rather than video, due to data management constraints - it's a large survey, in areas with poor internet connectivity, with a limited number of technical staff to process video. Photos will likely generated a smaller dataset (in terms of GB/TB), and be quicker to classify (AI classification for video is not yet widely available, but can be run locally for images), especially for non-technical staff (a folder based system with photos like the Sanderson workflow can be used by anyone able to use a computer), and measuring distances from a subset of photos will be quicker and simpler than finding specific frames within a video file and measuring at those points.

We had assumed that the burst mode on the cameras available would be something like Photo Mode 3 in this image, which I've shared on this group before: https://imgur.com/a/8u63uIq (apologies, images don't seem to paste in-line in this group).

However, following a pilot, it looks like it is closer to Photo Mode 2 in that image, as the delay between images within a burst vary between ~0.3 and ~0.6s, with the first 3 images of 5 being within the first second, and the following 2 of 5 taken around 0.6 second after that (i.e. photos captured at about :00.300, :00.600, :00.900, :01.500, and :02.100). A single image can be taken with burst mode off, with an interval of 0.6 seconds (i.e. at :00.600. :01.200, :01.800, :02.400, :03.000 etc), which would also reduce empty images compared to a 5-burst set up.

In addition, milliseconds are not recorded to the metadata by the camera trap firmware, making it difficult (or impossible) to know which image is closer to a snapshot, one taken 10ms before the snapshot, or 400 ms after the snapshot (as they are rounded to the second, or just have the milliseconds dropped, I'm not sure which).

We can still programmatically select images close/closest to the snapshot moment, which was the original intention, but the average difference between when the selected image was taken and the snapshot moment will be larger than anticipated, and have at least an element of structure (i.e. non-random, as it will be related to the initial trigger to a degree (but not always X seconds after the initial trigger, as the interval  (0.6) is not a integer or factor of t. This means detections will not necessarily be equally spaced by exactly 2 seconds, but may be 2 seconds +/- up to ~0.4s deviation.

So to reiterate my main question, and add some related ones:
Is there any estimate available on the size of this potential bias (snap shot moments not fully independent of initial capture)?
Is it likely to be small enough (with t = 2s) that it can be tolerated for the sake of practicality?
I assume the bias in our context would be smaller than in Cappelle et al. 2019 as, whilst not perfectly aligned with independent snapshot moments, the degree to which the detection distance is based on the moment of initial capture is reduced.
What might be the impact of using snapshot moments that are not equally spaced?
For example, selecting images closest to independent snapshot moments, but which end up being from e.g. :00.300, :01.800, :04.200 etc rather than on each second exactly.
Is there anything that could be done within the context above to reduce the potential bias as much as possible?
I assume decreasing t to 1s would help, but using images, the detections would still not be selected from a continuous range of times, but come from a set of quantized available images, as determined by the interval and trigger speed.

Thanks as always for your invaluable advice!

Cheers,

Olly

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] about group size assumptions
messages.body_plain:
Antonela

The phrase you quote from the first chapter of Buckland et al. (2015) is referring to the issue of size bias, whereby the average size of groups detected in a distance sampling survey is a biased estimate of the average size of groups in the population, because small groups at large distances are not detected in the field.  This is explained in our online workshop slides:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch5/L5-3%20Cluster%20Size.pdf

A regression approach is used in the Distance for Windows software to remove the size bias problem. (See the above PDF slides 7-8).

The ds() function in the R package Distance takes a different approach to this problem.  When group size is included as a covariate in the detection function, the effect of group size is incorporated into the estimation process.  A Horvitz-Thompson estimator is used to estimate both the number of groups and the number of individuals.  The ratio of those two estimates is a derived estimate of average group size in the population.

Have a look at this case study on our Examples page for a more detailed discussion.

http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-groupsize/Remedy-size-bias-for-dolphin-surveys.html

Hope that's useful.

messages.body_plain:
Carolin

You want to assess the fit of your detection function model to the observed detection distances.  If you are using Distance for Windows (I assume that is what you are using), fit can be assessed using the chi-square GOF test (assuming the distances are binned, as is common with camera trapping data):

If using the R package Distance, fit is assessed using the function `gof_ds()`.

The overdispersion addressed with the Poisson distribution is NOT the type of overdispersion associated with camera trapping data

This is relevant to variability in encounter rates between camera stations which relates to spatial clustering of animals through your study area.

Have a read through the paper by Howe et al. (2019) for matters of overdispersion as it relates to camera traps:
Howe, E. J., Buckland, S. T., Després‐Einspenner, M.-L., & Kühl, H. S. (2019). Model selection with overdispersed distance sampling data. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 10(1), 38–47. doi: 10.1111/2041-210X.13082 <https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13082>

and for an implementation of the model selection algorithm discussed in that paper, visit the case study on our website:

http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cameratraps/camera-distill.html#model-selection-adjustments-from-overdispersion

Spatially explicit models for distance sampling data: density surface
modelling in practice

8-12th March 2021 1600-1800 GMT//1100-1300 EST//0800-1000 PST

This online course will cover how to fit spatial models to distance
sampling data ("density surface modelling") in R. This will include:

- Brief overview of distance sampling

- Predicting abundance
- Making maps

Examples will be based around a line transect survey of sperm whales in
the western Atlantic.

The course will consist of 5 live sessions delivered over
videoconference. Between these sessions there will be practical R
exercises to complete and to assist with these practicals. Each

taken an introductory workshop in person or online (either interactively

using R.

messages.body_plain:
Really nice reply, Eric!

I come now with another question related to spatial aggregation of animals and overdispersion (in encounter rate).

When using Distance for Windows, how to deal in those situations in which we found overdispersion in encounter rate (between lines or points)?

Using the "unmarked" R package is possible to include negative binomial instead of Poission.  But, I think, that this is not possible in Distance for Windows. Buckland et al 2001  (section 3.6.1) suggested multiplication of the Poisson variance by two if no other approach for estimating variance was available.

Additionally, Buckland et al 2001  (section 4.4), recommended empirical estimation of the sampling variance of n,  as var(n) > E(n) is expected.

Are there other options included in the software? what is the approach that you recommend?

Thank you very much
Best
Pablo

El sábado, 12 de diciembre de 2020 a las 15:13:18 UTC+1, Eric Rexstad escribió:
>
> Carolin
>
> You want to assess the fit of your detection function model to the observed detection distances.  If you are using Distance for Windows (I assume that is what you are using), fit can be assessed using the chi-square GOF test (assuming the distances are binned, as is common with camera trapping data):
>
>
> If using the R package Distance, fit is assessed using the function `gof_ds()`.
>
> The overdispersion addressed with the Poisson distribution is NOT the type of overdispersion associated with camera trapping data
>
> This is relevant to variability in encounter rates between camera stations which relates to spatial clustering of animals through your study area.
>
> Have a read through the paper by Howe et al. (2019) for matters of overdispersion as it relates to camera traps:
> Howe, E. J., Buckland, S. T., Després‐Einspenner, M.-L., & Kühl, H. S. (2019). Model selection with overdispersed distance sampling data. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 10(1), 38–47. doi: 10.1111/2041-210X.13082 <https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13082>
>
> and for an implementation of the model selection algorithm discussed in that paper, visit the case study on our website:
>
> http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cameratraps/camera-distill.html#model-selection-adjustments-from-overdispersion
> On 12/12/2020 11:20, Carolin Klangwald wrote:
> > Hello everyone,
> > I`m a student working towards my Masters Thesis and new to the Distance software.
> > I`m trying to analyse camera trap data, which holds some overdispersion. Because of this I am not quite sure how to judge the goodness of fit. I`ve run several different analyses and the Halfnormal-Cosine with truncation seems to work well, and using the adjustment for a Poisson distribution with an overdispersion factor of 2 did result in improved accuracy. However I`m just not sure if I am handeling this appropriately. Does anyone have some suggestions for me or maybe could direct me to some sources?

messages.body_plain:
Pablo

There is a difference in the way Distance for Windows (and the R package Distance) deals with variability in encounter rate between transects, and the way this is handled using the 'unmarked' software.

The methods developed at St Andrews do not try to model transect-level encounters, so there is not a model (Poisson, negative binomial, ...) involved.  There is no concept of overdispersion in the absence of a model.  As you note in quoting Section 3.6.1 of Buckland et al. (2001), resorting to the Poisson approximation is only done if no other approach is available (see Section 4.7.1).  We recommend, as you note, that an empirical estimate of encounter rate variance be employed.  The veracity of this empirical estimate is strongly influenced by a sufficient number of spatial replicates in the form of transects.  A resampling approach (bootstrap) is usually employed to estimate uncertainty in abundance or density estimates, with the transect being the resampling unit.  Consequently, Buckland et al. (2001) Section 7.2.1 suggested 10-20 (or more) replicate transects be used for a reliable estimate of encounter rate variance.

If you want a more statistical treatment on the subject of estimating encounter rate variance, consult this Biometrics paper:
Fewster, R. M., Buckland, S. T., Burnham, K. P., Borchers, D. L., Jupp, P. E., Laake, J. L., & Thomas., L. (2009). Estimating the encounter rate variance in distance sampling. Biometrics, 65, 225–236. doi: 10.1111/j.1541-0420.2008.01018.x <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2008.01018.x>

The "R2" estimator (for line transects) from this paper is used as the default in Distance for Windows.  See Chapter 8 of the Distance for Windows users guide "Advanced analytical variance estimation in CDS"

messages.body_plain:
Mei-Ling

The preferred manner for resolving the size-bias issue (the mean size of your observed groups is a positively-biased estimates of the size of groups in the population because observers are likely to miss small groups at large distances) is via the covariate approach you describe.  This approach recognises detectability is a function both of distance from the transect and group size.

You could write your own code to perform the regression method (as I did in a question to the list back in 2017).  You can see the example here

https://groups.google.com/g/distance-sampling/c/2W7DJtaB82Q/m/4Ri2MLiiAAAJ

The difficult part of incorporating the result of the regression is to produce a measure of precision for mean group size; which is needed to propagate variability in estimated group size into the uncertainty in density of individuals.  The code in the link above takes a simple-minded approach to the uncertainty issue.

Regarding the formula you include for estimating density; that formula will produce an estimate of the density of *clusters* when detections are made of groups.  In that case, the 'n' in the formula would be the number of groups.

Mei-Ling

The "M2" approach you describe does not work, because when a covariate enters the detection function, there no longer is a single ESW.  Instead there is a different ESW for each group size; in other words, ESW is a function of group size, because detectability is a function of group size.

With group size as a covariate, a Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator is employed to estimate density of individuals.

Examine slide 14 of this set of lecture materials on covariates in the detection function

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch5/L5-4%20MCDS.pdf

To extend this framework to the case where group size is a covariate, examine slide 2 of

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch5/L5-5%20MCDS%20Complications.pdf

You could also listen to the lectures narrating those slides at the same website.

Recognise the interdependence between ESW and PaP_a.  Recognise ESW=Pa⋅wESW = P_a \cdot w, where w is truncation distance.  The PaP_a formulation is used by `ds()` and it fits smoothly into the Horvitz-Thompson-like framework.

I apologize if this question is rather basic but I cannot find a lot of information regarding the combination of smooth and parametric terms in the literature.

Thank you very much in advance!

Fitting GAMs is not my area of expertise, so take these comments with a large pinch of salt.

Inclusion of discrete (categorical) covariates in a GAM examines whether the shape of the smooths differ among levels of the discrete covariate; in effect looking at interaction between a smooth and a discrete covariate.

Have a look at Gavin Simpson's description of a case study including both discrete covariates and smooths

https://fromthebottomoftheheap.net/2017/12/14/difference-splines-ii/
